Full inventory, evidence-cited.

## 1. napi / platform packages

`crates/callisto-graph/src/napi.rs`:
- `triple_to_role(triple: &str) -> Option<ManifestRole>` (napi.rs:138) — matches exactly 18 hardcoded napi-rs triples (aarch64/x86_64-apple-darwin, 6 linux gnu/musl/gnueabihf, 3 windows-msvc, freebsd, 2 android, riscv64/ppc64/s390x-linux-gnu, 2 wasm) to `ManifestRole::Platform{platform,arch,abi}`. Unknown triple -> `None`, no default.
- `role_to_triple` (napi.rs:170) — exact reverse mapping, round-trip tested.
- `NapiTargetsIndex::load` (napi.rs:15) — per fixed-group, finds the first `Package` member, reads `<root>/<pkg-name>/package.json`'s `napi.targets` via `callisto_manifests::read_napi_targets`, **lenient**: malformed/non-array -> silently absent (`.ok().flatten()`).
- `napi_drift` (napi.rs:67) — diffs declared `napi.targets` vs actual `GroupMember::PlatformManifest` members, emits `NapiTargetAddedNotInMembers` / `NapiTargetRemovedStillOnDisk` warnings (both `Strict`-escalatable).

`crates/callisto-graph/src/matrix.rs` (backs `callisto matrix`, 1060 lines, doc: "Private helpers only -- public entry point is `crate::commands::matrix::matrix`"):
- `triple_host_runner_use_cross` (matrix.rs:12) — a SECOND, separate 18-triple table (same triples) mapping to CI `(hostRunner, useCross)`. Doc comment explicitly notes this cannot be derived from `triple_to_role`/`ManifestRole::Platform` since that carries no CI-scheduling concept — this is genuinely new code, not reuse.
- `artifact_name_for_package_platform` (matrix.rs:49) — `<sanitized-pkg-name>-<platform>-<arch>[-<abi>]`, `/` replaced with `-` (scoped npm names).
- `select_platform_target_source` (matrix.rs:260) — reads BOTH `napi.targets` (package.json) and `[tool.maturin].targets` (pyproject.toml) per package; both present -> hard error `ConflictingPlatformTargetSources`; exactly one (even empty array) -> `Ok(Some((PlatformTargetKind::{Napi,Maturin}, source_str, triples)))`. **This is the only place in the codebase maturin platform targets are read at all** — see point 2, there is no `ManifestRole::Platform` discovery for maturin.
- `build_matrix_report` -> `MatrixReport{platform_targets: BTreeMap<pkgname,PlatformTargetGroup>, runtime_versions: BTreeMap<pkgname,Vec<RuntimeVersionEntry>>, diagnostics}`. `runtime_versions` pulls `engines.node`/`requires-python` raw strings (npm-then-python order), no semver parsing.
- Consumer: `.github/actions/callisto-action/scripts/create-or-update-release-pr.sh:57-58`: `callisto matrix --format json | jq -c '[.platformTargets[].targets[]] | unique_by(.artifactName)'` -> action output `nativeMatrix` (action.yml:58-60, described as "Native build matrix preview"). **`grep -rn nativeMatrix .github/` finds NO consumer** — it's produced and exposed but nothing reads it. The actual release-artifact-preflight `matrix:` strategy blocks in `callisto-release.yml:268` and `callisto-ci.yml:127` are hardcoded YAML target lists, not generated from this. Treat `callisto matrix`/napi platform-target modeling as currently disconnected from the real build/publish pipeline.

## 2. ManifestRole::Platform

`crates/callisto-model/src/package.rs:109-117`:
```rust
pub enum ManifestRole {
    Canonical,
    Platform { platform: String, arch: String, abi: Option<String> },
    Lockfile,
}
```
`ManifestDecl::new` (package.rs:90-92) hard-rejects `Platform` role paired with `ManifestFormat::CargoToml` (Cargo has no platform-stub-package convention) — PyprojectToml is NOT rejected, so the type permits a Platform+PyprojectToml manifest, but nothing constructs one (see below).

Discovery path (the only one that exists): `walk.rs:174-176` builds `IdentityIndex.platform` exclusively from `Manifest::npm_role()` -> `NpmRole::Platform` (npm.rs-detected via package.json `os`+`cpu` arrays) — **npm-only**. `config/groups.rs:166-171` (`GroupTable::resolve`) turns `index.platform` entries named in `[[fixed-group]] members` into `GroupMember::PlatformManifest{owner,role,path,name}`. There is no Python/maturin equivalent anywhere in discovery — `select_platform_target_source`'s maturin read (point 1) is a standalone `callisto matrix`-only code path that never produces a `ManifestRole::Platform`/`GroupMember::PlatformManifest`.

`docs/01-spec.md` (searched around the SPEC DECISION for `Package`, found ~line 786 region):
> `[SPEC DECISION, not in 00-design.md: napi platform packages are ManifestRole::Platform manifests of the main Package, not separate Package values.]` §5.2 is authoritative here — "Case E (napi single package): one package, canonical manifests for the crate and the main JS package, N Platform manifests." ... This is what makes §13 invariant 20 ("platform manifests never receive an independent git tag") structural ... `is_release_point` below is a property of a `Package`, and platform manifests are not `Package`s.

So: a platform manifest is a non-canonical member manifest of the SAME `Package` (not its own release point, no independent tag), currently only ever populated for npm/napi.

## 3. PyPI support, actual extent

`Ecosystem::Pypi` IS in `Ecosystem::CANONICAL` (ecosystem.rs:30) and `is_implemented()` returns true (ecosystem.rs:81-83). What's real:
- `pyproject.toml` reading: `crates/callisto-manifests/src/python.rs` — full CST editor (`PyprojectToml`), PEP 621 / Poetry / Flit name+version extraction, Poetry caret/tilde/wildcard -> PEP440 range normalization, `is_publishable()` (false for nameless workspace-root pyproject.toml), `publish_targets()` -> `[PublishTarget::Pypi{index:None}]` when publishable.
- PEP 440: `Ecosystem::Pypi.version_grammar()` -> `VersionGrammar::Pep440` (ecosystem.rs:76), backed by `pep440_rs` (callisto-model dep).
- PEP 503 name normalization: `normalize_pypi_package_name`/`normalize_pypi_project_name` (ecosystem.rs:194-210).
- Build/publish: `registry_argv::pypi_publish_argv` (registry_argv.rs:288) runs `python -m build --sdist --wheel --outdir dist/` then `twine upload --skip-existing dist/<normalized-name>-<version>*` (optional `--repository-url` for private index). **This IS a real sdist+wheel build** but it's a plain, non-platform-tagged wheel (no cibuildwheel/maturin cross-compile, no per-triple wheel). `PypiPublish` struct flows through `commands/publish.rs` (lines 211,347,377-378,507-527).
- **Refusal, confirmed**: `crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/registry.rs:423-435`, `PypiRegistry::can_observe_versions()` returns `false`, with doc comment:
  > "pip cannot prove a PyPI version absent: an unreachable index and a project that does not exist produce the same message and the same exit code, `pip index versions` is experimental and hides yanked releases, and a pinned yanked release installs with only a warning. Declaring the truth here is what makes `require_observable_registry` refuse a PyPI publish at plan time rather than letting one reach a receipt it cannot support."
  The gate itself: `require_observable_registry` (registry.rs:486-492) — `GraphError::ReleasePreconditionUnmet{requirement: ObservableRegistryClient}` at plan time for any ecosystem whose adapter can't observe. **So PyPI publish is plan-time refused today, unconditionally** (not conditional on flags) — this is a hard current limitation, not merely a caveat.
- No wheel/sdist "concept" beyond the argv above — no `PlatformTargetKind::Maturin` cross-compile wiring into publish (maturin targets are read by `callisto matrix` only, never acted on for building real per-platform wheels).

## 4. Publish targets

`crates/callisto-model/src/ecosystem.rs:90-111`:
```rust
pub enum PublishTarget {
    CratesIo,
    Npm { registry: Option<String>, access: Option<NpmAccess> },
    Pypi { index: Option<String> },
    NuGet { source: Option<String> },
    GitHubRelease,
    None,
}
```
`is_implemented()` (ecosystem.rs:173-182): `None`->true (vacuous), `GitHubRelease`->false (hardcoded, no `Ecosystem` backing), `CratesIo`/`Npm`/`Pypi`/`NuGet` defer to `self.ecosystem().is_implemented()` -> only CratesIo/Npm/Pypi are actually true (NuGet ecosystem not in `is_implemented`'s match).

**No notion of "publish a platform package" distinct from the main package exists anywhere.** Platform manifests are never independent `Package`s (point 2) and are never given their own `PublishTarget`/`publish_to` — `is_release_point()` (package.rs:59-61) and all publish plumbing operate on `Package.publish_to`, and `Package.platform_manifests()` is excluded from anything publish/tag-related by construction (docs/01-spec.md invariant 20, quoted above). Confirmed via `crates/callisto-model/Cargo.toml` (license=MIT, no process/exec deps) and `crates/callisto-manifests/Cargo.toml` (license=**FSL-1.1-MIT**, so it's an FSL *product* crate, not one of the three MIT foundation crates — despite living conceptually "close to manifests"). Grep confirms `callisto-manifests` shells out to nothing (`grep -rn "Command::new|std::process|CommandRunner"` = empty).

Pattern already established, twice:
- `CommandRunner` trait itself (`crates/callisto-model/src/exec.rs:11`) is defined in the MIT-foundation `callisto-model` crate but is a **pure interface** (no actual subprocess code there) — real spawn/poll/kill implementations (`CliCommandRunner` etc.) live in FSL crates (`callisto-cli`, `callisto-graph`, `callisto-vcs`, `callisto-moon`) per `grep -rln "struct CliCommandRunner|impl CommandRunner for"`.
- `callisto-vcs` (an MIT foundation crate, ARCHITECTURE.md:264-296) itself shells out to `git` via its `ShellGit` backend using `CommandRunner` — so **shelling out is not itself restricted to FSL crates**; the CLAUDE.md rule is specifically "MIT foundation crates must never depend on FSL *product* crates," not "must do no I/O."

This is a **product-crate** (`callisto-graph`, FSL) trait, sitting in `commands/release/provider/`, one adapter per `Ecosystem`, selected via `adapter_for(ecosystem: Ecosystem)` (registry.rs:203).

**Recommendation**: a new capability resolver that runs e.g. `rustc --print cfg` belongs in `callisto-graph` (FSL product crate), most naturally as a sibling trait to `RegistryEcosystem` under `commands/release/provider/` (or a new adjacent module if it's not release-specific) — same shape: one trait, per-`Ecosystem` adapters, shelling out via the existing `CommandRunner` (from `callisto-model`) rather than raw `std::process::Command`. Do NOT put it in `callisto-manifests` (FSL but currently I/O-free by convention/precedent — every existing manifest editor is pure CST manipulation, no subprocess) or in `callisto-model`/`callisto-vcs` (MIT foundation; only acceptable there if the trait is a pure interface with zero product-crate knowledge, mirroring `CommandRunner` itself).

Both objections are answerable — the refusal is about **pip**, not about PyPI.

- `info.yanked` and `yanked_reason` are exposed in the JSON API, so yanked releases are visible rather than hidden.
- The PEP 503 simple index gives the same 200/404 and is the one endpoint *any* index must implement, so it works for private indexes where the warehouse JSON API doesn't.

So `PypiRegistry::can_observe_versions() → false` rests on accurate reasoning about `pip index versions` that got generalized into a false conclusion about the registry. Same shape as the other two we found today: a correct observation about one mechanism, stated as a property of the capability.

**Honest gaps in what I just proved:** I tested pypi.org only, and `requests 2.31.0` isn't yanked — so I've confirmed the field *exists*, not that it populates on a genuinely yanked release. That needs a known-yanked version before anyone builds on it.

**And there's a real cost**, which is probably why it went this way: `callisto-graph` has **no HTTP client**. Every provider shells out to `cargo`, `npm` or `gh`. Observing PyPI means either shelling `curl` (present on GH runners, not guaranteed elsewhere) or adding an HTTP client to the release path — which this codebase has deliberately avoided, and which the `registry_endpoint.rs` https restriction was written around.

So Python isn't walled off; it's a scoped decision with a real dependency question attached.

That makes the scoping question sharper, and it's yours:

1. **rust + napi now, python recorded** — smallest, and napi is where the disconnected machinery already is.
2. **all three**, accepting an HTTP dependency in the release path for PyPI observation.
3. **rust + napi now, python as a spike** — settle the yanked case and the curl-vs-client question before committing.

Whichever you pick, the napi work is the same and it's the bigger win: connecting `callisto matrix` to the workflows so a target is one config line instead of five hand-copies, and giving platform sub-packages a publish path they currently don't have at all.
Is there a better way to architect and handle this? How do other tools do this? Are we doing something novel? Are we overengineering it?

Straight answers.

## Are we doing something novel?

The combination, yes. Nobody does all of it:

| tool | versioning + cascade | registry publish | binary artifacts | provenance | recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| changesets | npm only | yes | no | no | no |
| release-please | multi-lang | no | no | no | no |
| nx release | yes | yes | no | no | no |
| cargo-dist | no | no | yes | attestation | no |
| goreleaser | no | some | yes | some | no |
| **callisto** | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |

The genuinely novel part is treating a release as a **state machine with evidence** — observe before effect, durable state, receipts. Everyone else treats release as fire-and-forget. That's real, and it's why 0.8.0 recovered cleanly from a half-published state this morning instead of needing manual repair.

## Are we overengineering it?

Yes, in a specific and diagnosable way: **depth in the model, gaps in the wiring.**

- A 1,197-scenario fault simulator, evidence-carrying observation types, a transition table — and none of them caught any of the five bugs that actually broke the release. All five were shell glue and platform semantics.
- `callisto matrix`: 18-triple table, `artifactName` derivation, drift detection, ~35 tests. **Zero consumers.** The real matrices are hardcoded YAML.
- Three separate target tables for one domain.
- PyPI refused at plan time on reasoning that's correct about `pip` and wrong about PyPI.

The tell is that the elaborate parts are inert while the load-bearing parts are hand-copied.

## How do others handle multi-ecosystem?

**They don't unify it.** release-please uses per-language *strategies* with a shared PR/changelog shell. nx uses pluggable `versionActions`, default JS, non-JS supplies its own. cibuildwheel sits *above* builders and delegates the build entirely.

Nobody builds a universal target abstraction — because the vocabularies genuinely don't unify. We proved that today: napi's `platformArchABI` is a hand-maintained lookup in Node's vocabulary, and wheel tags need a glibc-policy decision with no Rust equivalent.

## So: my `TargetFacts` seam was mild overengineering

It abstracts over things that share almost nothing. The only genuinely shared fact is *"cargo produced a binary for triple T."* Everything after is ecosystem-specific packaging — which is exactly what `napi build` and `maturin` already are.

**The better architecture is to delegate the build and own the orchestration.** Callisto's differentiator is the state machine, provenance and monorepo cascade — not compiling binaries. You already do this for the CLI: `build-release-artifact.sh` shells `cargo build` and `tar`. Extend that shape — invoke `napi build`, invoke `maturin build`, model only the *outputs* and where they go — rather than reimplementing their target knowledge.

That collapses "comprehensive three-ecosystem support" into: a declared build command per artifact, and a declared destination. No `TargetFacts`, no triple tables, no `rustc --print cfg`. The ecosystems keep their own weirdness, which they're better at maintaining than you are.

The one thing I'd still fix regardless is the product-identity hardcode — that's not architecture, it's a bug.

Npm: `["view", "NAME@VER", "--json"]` (+`--registry` if configured) (:361-373); exit0+empty stdout -> `Absent`, exit0+nonempty -> `Exact`; exit!=0 + stderr/stdout containing e404/etarget/"no matching version"/"is not in this registry" -> `Absent`; else -> transient `Indeterminate(CommandFailed)`.

## 2. HTTP constraint
Confirmed: `crates/callisto-graph/Cargo.toml` has no http client dep, every provider shells out. **But GitHub releases already do exactly this via HTTP**: `github.rs` runs `gh api --include METHOD endpoint` (github.rs:37, policy.rs `programs::GH="gh"`) and parses the raw response with `provider/http.rs::parse_http_response` (status line + headers + blank line + body — byte-identical to `curl -i` framing). `registry_endpoint.rs` forces registry URLs to `https://` only (no loopback exception) — irrelevant to which shell tool we pick, but confirms prod traffic is always TLS.
**Recommend: shell `curl -sS -i`.** Reuses `http::parse_http_response`/`HttpResponse` verbatim (same framing as `gh api --include`), zero new parsing code. Tradeoffs: `curl` — ubiquitous on GH runners and virtually every dev box, not memory-guaranteed on minimal containers (one sentence: fine given `gh`/`git`/`cargo`/`npm` are already assumed-present externals). `python -m pip`/`python -c` — pip is already a PyPI-ecosystem dependency the user has installed for `python -m build`/`twine`, but its JSON output is unstable/undocumented and `pip index versions` is explicitly experimental (the doc comment we're overturning). Endpoint: PEP 503/691 simple index, JSON-negotiated: `curl -sS -i -H "Accept: application/vnd.pypi.simple.v1+json" {base}/{normalize_pypi_project_name(name)}/`. `base` = `operation.registry.endpoint` when `Some` (binding.rs:88-99 leaves this `None` for default PyPI; existing `pypi_publish_argv` already treats a configured registry url as this same index-shaped string — reuse it, don't invent a second URL), else default `https://pypi.org/simple`. Transport failure (curl nonzero exit, no HTTP response parsed) -> transient `Indeterminate(CommandFailed)`, mirroring `github_api_response`'s "keep the command failure only when no parseable HTTP response exists" rule (github.rs:52-66).

## Forge roles and DAG order (`provider/forge.rs`, `provider/artifact.rs`)

Publication is the last forge step, because GitHub releases can be immutable:
once published, assets can no longer be added, so a release must be complete
before it is published.

`Tag` -> `ForgeRelease` (create as draft) -> every `ArtifactUpload` -> `ForgePublish`.
`ForgePublish` depends on the draft and on *every* upload of that release,
including when there are none.

- `ForgeRelease` effect: `gh release create TAG --repo R --verify-tag --draft
  --generate-notes`, plus `--prerelease` when the released version has a semver
  pre-release part (`Version::is_prerelease()`, the same source as the npm
  `next` dist-tag).
- `ForgePublish` effect: `gh release edit TAG --repo R --draft=false`.
- Lookup: `GET /releases/tags/{tag}` omits drafts, so a 404 there is followed by
  a bounded scan of `GET /releases?per_page=100&page=N` (at most 10 pages).
  Both roles and the upload role share this one lookup.
- `ForgeRelease` is `Exact` for a draft or a published release; `ForgePublish`
  is `Exact` only when `draft: false` and `Absent` while still a draft. A
  release whose tag matches but whose `prerelease` flag disagrees with the
  version is `Conflict { ForgeReleasePrereleaseDiffers }`.
- Uploads target the draft, compare by size and `sha256` digest, and never pass
  `--clobber`. An asset missing from a published release is `Absent`, so it is
  uploaded; an immutable release refuses that upload as a typed command failure
  rather than letting the release be reported complete.

== .changeset/release-product-artifacts.md
---
callisto-cli: minor
---

**Recoverable, validated product releases**

`callisto release` now recovers interrupted releases from provider observation (registry, remote tag, forge release, assets) and validates arguments and the receipt path before any effect. One profile authority governs execution (E198). `previous-tag-templates` keeps renamed tags discoverable, and the CLI product tag is now `callisto@{version}`. The `[release]` table configures product artifacts and a qualified `product-package`, with canonical destination isolation and per-command deadlines. Sources without a `[release]` plan get zero artifact slots and a notice. Registry observation goes through the ecosystem package manager, so registry resolution and authentication (including private registries) are handled by the same tool and configuration the publish uses: cargo is observed with `cargo info NAME@VERSION --registry REGISTRY` run from the workspace root, npm with `npm view`. A registry endpoint must now be `https`, with no loopback exception. PyPI publish targets are refused at plan time, because pip cannot distinguish a missing project from an unreachable index and so can never prove a version absent. A yanked crate version reads as absent (`cargo info` cannot see yanks) and the publish that follows fails closed with the typed unconfirmed-publication error rather than producing a receipt. Transient registry and forge failures (429, 5xx, rate-limited 403, timeouts, unreachable registries) are retried with bounded exponential backoff that honours `Retry-After`, instead of aborting the release. The GitHub Release is now created as a draft and published only after every product asset has been uploaded to it, so a release is never visible without its assets and an interrupted run cannot leave a published, incomplete release behind; release intents planned by an earlier version must be re-planned.

---
callisto-moon: patch
---

**Restore the dependency audit baseline**

`callisto-moon`'s dependency tree pinned `rustls 0.23.43`, affected by [RUSTSEC-2026-0285](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0285), and the yanked `chacha20 0.10.1`. Update both transitive dependencies to audited releases without moving unrelated packages.
== .changeset/registry-confirmation-ecosystem-gate.md
---
callisto-graph: patch
---

**Extract the registry-confirmation ecosystem gate into a single, testable source of truth**

`dispatch_registry` decided which ecosystems get a post-publish registry-confirmation check inline, in the same match arm that ran the check itself -- so nothing directly proved Cargo was actually wired in (only the classification logic it calls was unit-tested). That's exactly the shape of gap that let Cargo's confirmation go missing in the first place.

The decision is now its own pure function, `ecosystem_requires_registry_confirmation`, which `dispatch_registry` calls directly rather than re-deciding inline. A test on that function is now a direct proof of the runtime gate, not a parallel copy of it -- verified by temporarily reintroducing the original gap and confirming the test catches it.

content.text:
# Update Config Skill

Modify Claude Code configuration by updating settings.json files.

## When Hooks Are Required (Not Memory)

If the user wants something to happen automatically in response to an EVENT, they need a **hook** configured in settings.json. Memory/preferences cannot trigger automated actions.

**These require hooks:**
- "Before compacting, ask me what to preserve" → PreCompact hook
- "After writing files, run prettier" → PostToolUse hook with Write|Edit matcher
- "When I run bash commands, log them" → PreToolUse hook with Bash matcher
- "Always run tests after code changes" → PostToolUse hook

**Hook events:** PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, Stop, Notification, SessionStart

## CRITICAL: Read Before Write

**Always read the existing settings file before making changes.** Merge new settings with existing ones - never replace the entire file.

## CRITICAL: Use AskUserQuestion for Ambiguity

When the user's request is ambiguous, use AskUserQuestion to clarify:
- Which settings file to modify (user/project/local)
- Whether to add to existing arrays or replace them
- Specific values when multiple options exist

## Decision: /config command vs Direct Edit

**Suggest the `/config` slash command** for these simple settings:
- `theme`, `editorMode`, `verbose`, `model`
- `language`, `alwaysThinkingEnabled`
- `permissions.defaultMode`

**Edit settings.json directly** for:
- Hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, etc.)
- Complex permission rules (allow/deny arrays)
- Environment variables
- MCP server configuration
- Plugin configuration

## Workflow

1. **Clarify intent** - Ask if the request is ambiguous
2. **Read existing file** - Use Read tool on the target settings file
3. **Merge carefully** - Preserve existing settings, especially arrays
4. **Edit file** - Use Edit tool (if file doesn't exist, ask user to create it first)
5. **Confirm** - Tell user what was changed

## Merging Arrays (Important!)

When adding to permission arrays or hook arrays, **merge with existing**, don't replace:

**WRONG** (replaces existing permissions):
```json
{ "permissions": { "allow": ["Bash(npm *)"] } }
```

**RIGHT** (preserves existing + adds new):
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": [
      "Bash(git *)",      // existing
      "Edit(.claude)",    // existing
      "Bash(npm *)"       // new
    ]
  }
}
```

## Settings File Locations

Choose the appropriate file based on scope:

| File | Scope | Git | Use For |
|------|-------|-----|---------|
| `~/.claude/settings.json` | Global | N/A | Personal preferences for all projects |
| `.claude/settings.json` | Project | Commit | Team-wide hooks, permissions, plugins |
| `.claude/settings.local.json` | Project | Gitignore | Personal overrides for this project |

Settings load in order: user → project → local (later overrides earlier).

## Settings Schema Reference

### Permissions
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm *)", "Edit(.claude)", "Read"],
    "deny": ["Bash(rm -rf *)"],
    "ask": ["Edit(//etc/*)"],
    "defaultMode": "default" | "plan" | "acceptEdits" | "dontAsk",
    "additionalDirectories": ["/extra/dir"]
  }
}
```

**Permission Rule Syntax:**
- Exact match: `"Bash(npm run test)"`
- Prefix wildcard: `"Bash(git *)"` - matches `git`, `git status`, `git commit`, etc.
- Tool only: `"Read"` - allows all Read operations
- File paths: `"Edit(src/**)"` - path rules in `permissions` use `Edit(path)` for every file-writing tool (Write, Edit, NotebookEdit) and `Read(path)` for reads. `Write(path)`, `NotebookEdit(path)` and `Glob(path)` rules are not matched by file permission checks. Bare tool names (`"Write"`), deny/ask `Tool(param:value)` rules and hook `if` conditions still use each tool's own name

### Environment Variables
```json
{
  "env": {
    "DEBUG": "true",
    "MY_API_KEY": "value"
  }
}
```

### Model & Agent
```json
{
  "model": "sonnet",  // or "fable", "opus", "haiku", full model ID
  "agent": "agent-name",
  "alwaysThinkingEnabled": true
}
```

### Attribution (Commits & PRs)
```json
{
  "attribution": {
    "commit": "Custom commit trailer text",
    "pr": "Custom PR description text"
  }
}
```
Set `commit` or `pr` to empty string `""` to hide that attribution.

### MCP Server Management
```json
{
  "enableAllProjectMcpServers": true,
  "enabledMcpjsonServers": ["server1", "server2"],
  "disabledMcpjsonServers": ["blocked-server"]
}
```

### Plugins
```json
{
  "enabledPlugins": {
    "formatter@anthropic-tools": true
  }
}
```
Plugin syntax: `plugin-name@source` where source is `claude-code-marketplace`, `claude-plugins-official`, or `builtin`.

### Other Settings
- `language`: Preferred response language (e.g., "japanese")
- `cleanupPeriodDays`: Days to keep transcripts before automatic cleanup (default: 30; minimum 1)
- `respectGitignore`: Whether to respect .gitignore (default: true)
- `spinnerTipsEnabled`: Show tips in spinner
- `timeFormat`: Clock format for times shown in the UI: "auto" (default), "12-hour", "24-hour", "24-hour-utc", or a strftime pattern such as "%H:%M"
- `timeZone`: IANA time zone for times shown in the UI, e.g. "UTC" (default: system time zone)
- `spinnerVerbs`: Customize spinner verbs (`{ "mode": "append" | "replace", "verbs": [...] }`)
- `spinnerTipsOverride`: Override spinner tips (`{ "excludeDefault": true, "tips": ["Custom tip"] }`)
- `syntaxHighlightingDisabled`: Disable diff highlighting


## Hooks Configuration

Hooks run commands at specific points in Claude Code's lifecycle.

### Hook Structure
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "EVENT_NAME": [
      {
        "matcher": "ToolName|OtherTool",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "your-command-here",
            "timeout": 60,
            "statusMessage": "Running..."
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Hook Events

| Event | Matcher | Purpose |
|-------|---------|---------|
| PermissionRequest | Tool name | Run before permission prompt |
| PreToolUse | Tool name | Run before tool, can block |
| PostToolUse | Tool name | Run after successful tool |
| PostToolUseFailure | Tool name | Run after tool fails |
| Notification | Notification type | Run on notifications |
| Stop | - | Run when Claude stops (including clear, resume, compact) |
| PreCompact | "manual"/"auto" | Before compaction |
| PostCompact | "manual"/"auto" | After compaction (receives summary) |
| UserPromptSubmit | - | When user submits |
| SessionStart | - | When session starts |

**Common tool matchers:** `Bash`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Read`, `Glob`, `Grep`

### Hook Types

**1. Command Hook** - Runs a shell command:
```json
{ "type": "command", "command": "prettier --write $FILE", "timeout": 30 }
```

**2. Prompt Hook** - Evaluates a condition with LLM:
```json
{ "type": "prompt", "prompt": "Is this safe? $ARGUMENTS" }
```
Only available for tool events: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest.

**3. Agent Hook** - Runs an agent with tools:
```json
{ "type": "agent", "prompt": "Verify tests pass: $ARGUMENTS" }
```
Only available for tool events: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest.

### Hook Input (stdin JSON)
```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "tool_name": "Write",
  "tool_input": { "file_path": "/path/to/file.txt", "content": "..." },
  "tool_response": { "success": true }  // PostToolUse only
}
```

### Hook JSON Output

Hooks can return JSON to control behavior:

```json
{
  "systemMessage": "Warning shown to user in UI",
  "continue": false,
  "stopReason": "Message shown when blocking",
  "suppressOutput": false,
  "decision": "block",
  "reason": "Explanation for decision",
  "hookSpecificOutput": {
    "hookEventName": "PostToolUse",
    "additionalContext": "Context injected back to model"
  }
}
```

**Fields:**
- `systemMessage` - Display a message to the user (all hooks)
- `continue` - Set to `false` to block/stop (default: true)
- `stopReason` - Message shown when `continue` is false
- `suppressOutput` - Hide stdout from transcript (default: false)
- `decision` - "block" for PostToolUse/Stop/UserPromptSubmit hooks (deprecated for PreToolUse, use hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision instead)
- `reason` - Explanation for decision
- `hookSpecificOutput` - Event-specific output (must include `hookEventName`):
  - `additionalContext` - Text injected into model context
  - `permissionDecision` - "allow", "deny", or "ask" (PreToolUse only)
  - `permissionDecisionReason` - Reason for the permission decision (PreToolUse only)
  - `updatedInput` - Modified tool input (PreToolUse only)

### Common Patterns

**Auto-format after writes:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_response.filePath // .tool_input.file_path' | { read -r f; prettier --write \"$f\"; } 2>/dev/null || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

**Log all bash commands:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.command' >> ~/.claude/bash-log.txt"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

**Stop hook that displays message to user:**

Command must output JSON with `systemMessage` field:
```bash
# Example command that outputs: {"systemMessage": "Session complete!"}
echo '{"systemMessage": "Session complete!"}'
```

**Run tests after code changes:**
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path // .tool_response.filePath' | grep -E '\\.(ts|js)$' && npm test || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```


## Constructing a Hook (with verification)

Given an event, matcher, target file, and desired behavior, follow this flow. Each step catches a different failure class — a hook that silently does nothing is worse than no hook.

1. **Dedup check.** Read the target file. If a hook already exists on the same event+matcher, show the existing command and ask: keep it, replace it, or add alongside.

2. **Construct the command for THIS project — don't assume.** The hook receives JSON on stdin. Build a command that:
   - Extracts any needed payload safely — use `jq -r` into a quoted variable or `{ read -r f; ... "$f"; }`, NOT unquoted `| xargs` (splits on spaces)
   - Invokes the underlying tool the way this project runs it (npx/bunx/yarn/pnpm? Makefile target? globally-installed?)
   - Skips inputs the tool doesn't handle (formatters often have `--ignore-unknown`; if not, guard by extension)
   - Stays RAW for now — no `|| true`, no stderr suppression. You'll wrap it after the pipe-test passes.

3. **Pipe-test the raw command.** Synthesize the stdin payload the hook will receive and pipe it directly:
   - `Pre|PostToolUse` on `Write|Edit`: `echo '{"tool_name":"Edit","tool_input":{"file_path":"<a real file from this repo>"}}' | <cmd>`
   - `Pre|PostToolUse` on `Bash`: `echo '{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"ls"}}' | <cmd>`
   - `Stop`/`UserPromptSubmit`/`SessionStart`: most commands don't read stdin, so `echo '{}' | <cmd>` suffices

   Check exit code AND side effect (file actually formatted, test actually ran). If it fails you get a real error — fix (wrong package manager? tool not installed? jq path wrong?) and retest. Once it works, wrap with `2>/dev/null || true` (unless the user wants a blocking check).

4. **Write the JSON.** Merge into the target file (schema shape in the "Hook Structure" section above). If this creates `.claude/settings.local.json` for the first time, add it to .gitignore — the Write tool doesn't auto-gitignore it.

5. **Validate syntax + schema in one shot:**

   `jq -e '.hooks.<event>[] | select(.matcher == "<matcher>") | .hooks[] | select(.type == "command") | .command' <target-file>`

   Exit 0 + prints your command = correct. Exit 4 = matcher doesn't match. Exit 5 = malformed JSON or wrong nesting. A broken settings.json silently disables ALL settings from that file — fix any pre-existing malformation too.

6. **Prove the hook fires** — only for `Pre|PostToolUse` on a matcher you can trigger in-turn (`Write|Edit` via Edit, `Bash` via Bash). `Stop`/`UserPromptSubmit`/`SessionStart` fire outside this turn — skip to step 7.

   For a **formatter** on `PostToolUse`/`Write|Edit`: introduce a detectable violation via Edit (two consecutive blank lines, bad indentation, missing semicolon — something this formatter corrects; NOT trailing whitespace, Edit strips that before writing), re-read, confirm the hook **fixed** it. For **anything else**: temporarily prefix the command in settings.json with `echo "$(date) hook fired" >> /tmp/claude-hook-check.txt; `, trigger the matching tool (Edit for `Write|Edit`, a harmless `true` for `Bash`), read the sentinel file.

   **Always clean up** — revert the violation, strip the sentinel prefix — whether the proof passed or failed.

   **If proof fails but pipe-test passed and `jq -e` passed**: the settings watcher isn't watching `.claude/` — it only watches directories that had a settings file when this session started. The hook is written correctly. Tell the user to open `/hooks` once (reloads config) or restart — you can't do this yourself; `/hooks` is a user UI menu and opening it ends this turn.

7. **Handoff.** Tell the user the hook is live (or needs `/hooks`/restart per the watcher caveat). Point them at `/hooks` to review, edit, or disable it later. The UI only shows "Ran N hooks" if a hook errors or is slow — silent success is invisible by design.


## Example Workflows

### Adding a Hook

User: "Format my code after Claude writes it"

1. **Clarify**: Which formatter? (prettier, gofmt, etc.)
2. **Read**: `.claude/settings.json` (or create if missing)
3. **Merge**: Add to existing hooks, don't replace
4. **Result**:
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write|Edit",
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "command",
        "command": "jq -r '.tool_response.filePath // .tool_input.file_path' | { read -r f; prettier --write \"$f\"; } 2>/dev/null || true"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

### Adding Permissions

User: "Allow npm commands without prompting"

1. **Read**: Existing permissions
2. **Merge**: Add `Bash(npm *)` to allow array
3. **Result**: Combined with existing allows

### Environment Variables

User: "Set DEBUG=true"

1. **Decide**: User settings (global) or project settings?
2. **Read**: Target file
3. **Merge**: Add to env object
```json
{ "env": { "DEBUG": "true" } }
```

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. **Replacing instead of merging** - Always preserve existing settings
2. **Wrong file** - Ask user if scope is unclear
3. **Invalid JSON** - Validate syntax after changes
4. **Forgetting to read first** - Always read before write

## Troubleshooting Hooks

If a hook isn't running:
1. **Check the settings file** - Read ~/.claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.json
2. **Verify JSON syntax** - Invalid JSON silently fails
3. **Check the matcher** - Does it match the tool name? (e.g., "Bash", "Write", "Edit")
4. **Check hook type** - Is it "command", "prompt", or "agent"?
5. **Test the command** - Run the hook command manually to see if it works
6. **Use --debug** - Run `claude --debug` to see hook execution logs

```json
      "description": "Price usage at your organization's contracted rates instead of list price. Affects every spend figure Claude Code reports — /cost, the status line, the SDK total_cost_usd, --max-budget-usd, and the OpenTelemetry cost metric and events — which remain USD estimates, not an invoice (the per-Mtok price labels in /model stay at list). \"overrides\" maps a model ID to its USD-per-million-token rates (input, output, cacheRead, cacheWrite — all four required, each 0 to 10000; cacheWrite prices both 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes). A matching row is charged exactly as written; fast-mode and US-data-residency surcharges are not added on top. A key Claude Code itself uses for a built-in model — its ID such as \"claude-sonnet-4-6\", or its first-party, Bedrock (any or no region prefix), Vertex or Foundry ID — covers every dated and provider form of that model; any other key — a gateway model alias, or a spelling Claude Code does not itself use — matches that model ID only (case-insensitive), and such an exact match wins over a built-in row. On Bedrock an application inference profile is matched by its backing model.               },

                "type": "number",
                "minimum": 0,
                "maximum": 10000
              },
              "cacheRead": {
```

PyPI applies to `callisto publish` only. The durable release lifecycle
(`callisto release plan` / `execute`, see `07-self-release-lifecycle.md`) refuses a PyPI publish
target at plan time: pip cannot distinguish a missing project from an unreachable index, so a PyPI
version can never be proved absent and a durable release could never confirm one.

Python publishing uses `twine upload`. Twine reads credentials from two environment
variables: `TWINE_USERNAME` (set to `__token__` when using a PyPI API token) and
`TWINE_PASSWORD` (set to the API token value). Set these in the job environment before
----
publish that follows is refused by the registry, and since only an exact observation may satisfy an
operation, the run ends in the typed unconfirmed-publication error rather than in a receipt.

PyPI is not supported by durable release. `pip` cannot prove a version absent — an unreachable
index and a project that does not exist produce identical output and the same exit code,
`pip index versions` is experimental and hides yanked releases, and a pinned yanked release
installs with only a warning. A PyPI publish target is therefore refused at plan time (E170), with a
message naming the reason and the alternatives: publish it outside durable release, or wait for a
reliable PyPI observation.

content.text:
Confirmed: pnpm selects the package with `--filter=<name>`. The agent's other claims check out too.

**napi support is broken at the model level, not just missing a publish path.** In real repos this breaks three ways:

1. **Invariant 20 is already violated.** In the standard layout (`npm/darwin-arm64/package.json`, no `Cargo.toml` beside it), `walk.rs:157-183` gives every npm manifest a Canonical decl and adds Platform on top. So each platform package becomes its own `Package`, a release point, and gets its own tag and GitHub release. The spec (`docs/01-spec.md` Case E) says these must be manifests of the main addon. The code never implemented that for this layout.
2. **Publishing selects by name from the workspace root** (`npm --workspace=`, `pnpm --filter=`, `yarn workspace`). napi's `npm/*` directories usually aren't workspace members, so publishing a platform package would fail. It needs to publish from the directory (`npm publish <dir>`).
3. **The main addon's npm name comes from the crate** (`addon`, not `@s/addon`), so the main npm publish probably targets the wrong package today. This is the agent's finding from a throwaway test; I haven't reproduced it.

None of this surfaced because no napi project has ever run Callisto. The fan-out I specced would have double-published or hung off the wrong owner. The agent was right to stop.

The fix is to implement Case E as the spec already describes: attach standalone platform `package.json` files to their main addon, publish platform packages by directory, and take the npm name from `package.json`. That changes package discovery, which versioning, groups and tags all depend on. It needs a realistic napi-rs fixture to test against, and it's a bigger change than the other six PRs.

My recommendation: merge the six open PRs first, since they're independent and green. Then run napi as its own change: an opus agent in a worktree, working from a real napi-rs layout, with (1) as the priority since it's an invariant break. I'll add it to the v1 plan in the meantime. content.text:
Your intuition about the concept is right, but #107 doesn't break anything. Two different things share the name:

- **`callisto matrix`**, the CLI command, is what drives build jobs, and it's untouched. michi uses it exactly that way: its own workflow step runs `callisto matrix --format json` (`release.yml:58`), exports the result as `nativeMatrix` (`:59`), and feeds its build job via `fromJson(...)` (`:72`).
- **callisto-action's `nativeMatrix` output** is what #107 removed. It re-ran the same command, but only in the `noop` branch — "no changesets, nothing to release" — and never when a release PR was actually created or updated. So it could never hand a matrix to a build.

Checked your downstream repos: michi computes its own matrix (unaffected), oxc-react-codegen uses callisto-action but never reads that output, and callisto itself doesn't either.

Two things I noticed while looking, not fixed:

- michi pins `callisto-action@main` (`release.yml:131`), so it silently picks up every change, including #107 once merged. oxc pins a commit, which is safer.
- michi's workflow comment refers to "callisto-action's own placement step (0.5.0+)". An earlier check found no such step in the action script, so that comment is probably stale.
We will pin versions once we have safe versions

Makes sense. Until then, anything merged to main reaches michi on its next run. So the six PRs are effectively live the moment they merge, which is one more reason they're each kept green and independent.

The npm platform-publish agent is still running. I'll report when it lands.

content.text:
E2E tests use a fake `cargo` script, so their cost is callisto's own **real** backoff sleeps (2+4+8+16 = 30s per exhausted retry), which matches the 39–40s tests.

**Findings, all measured.** On macOS CI, test execution is 427s. Compile is only 1m23s, so the rust-cache works. The time is waiting, not computing:

| cause | evidence | fix | risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| cargo's own `net.retry` inside each of callisto's 5 attempts | 11s → 0s per `cargo info` with `net.retry=0`; the 58s unit test | set `CARGO_NET_RETRY=0` in the test fixture | none |
| real backoff sleeps in CLI e2e tests | 30s per exhausted retry; the 39–40s tests; `release_hardening_tests` sums to 279s | a test-only env knob that scales the `ThreadSleeper` backoff | low |
| each moon test process rebuilds the wasm | `Once` doesn't span nextest processes; one test takes 109s | build the wasm once in a CI step before nextest | none |
| unoptimized wasmtime in debug builds | ~17s per moon test | `[profile.dev.package.cranelift-codegen] opt-level = 3` (plus its regalloc) | slower cold dep build once, then cached |

My estimate is that this cuts test execution from ~7 min to ~2–3 min on macOS. Coverage (5 min) and your local `cargo test` runs benefit the same way, since they run the same slow tests. It's an estimate until measured after the change.

**Production issue found along the way:** callisto's bounded retry wraps cargo's internal retry, so an unreachable registry takes about a minute before reporting indeterminate. Passing `--config net.retry=0` to `cargo info` would let callisto own the retry policy alone. That changes how transient errors are handled in production, so it's your call rather than something to fold in quietly.

PR #112: `strip = true` in `[profile.release]`.

**Verified:**
- The 0.8.0 CLI we shipped was already a real prod build (LTO, `opt-level=3`, `codegen-units=1`, no debug info). The only leftover was the symbol table.

**Not verified:** that the wasm name section is removed. I'd need to add the `wasm32-wasip1` target to your local toolchain to check.

**One place still builds debug, deliberately:** `setup-callisto` with `source: local` runs `cargo build` without `--release`. The release workflow uses that binary internally to plan and execute; nothing built that way is shipped. Switching it to release would add several minutes of LTO compile to each of about four release jobs. I'd leave it unless you want the runner to use the same optimized binary it ships.

- The production `net.retry` question.

input.description: Keep npm access through publish-to overrides
input.name: impl-npm-access
input.prompt:
Callisto repo, isolated worktree. Implement. Terse report.
GIT: use /opt/homebrew/bin/git for every git command. If refused, STOP and report.
`/opt/homebrew/bin/git fetch origin && /opt/homebrew/bin/git checkout -B fix/publish-to-keeps-npm-access origin/main`

Defect (found while enabling oxc-react-docgen's npm release): an explicit `[[package]] publish-to = ["npm"]` override in callisto.toml REPLACES the manifest-derived publish targets, so `PublishTarget::Npm { registry, access }` loses `access` read from package.json `publishConfig.access` (it becomes None). Scoped packages then publish with npm's default (restricted) and a first public publish fails. The same access is reused for platform packages (PlatformPublish ops) under that owner.

Fix: when a config override names `npm`, merge in the manifest's `publishConfig.access` (and `publishConfig.registry` if that's also read today — check) unless the config itself specifies them. Config wins when explicit; manifest fills gaps. Find where overrides are applied (config/resolve.rs parse_publish_target, walk.rs where Package.publish_to is built, callisto-manifests npm.rs publish_targets). Mirror for any other ecosystem field dropped the same way — check PyPI index — and fix or record.

Also consider: should callisto default scoped npm packages to access=public when nothing says otherwise? Do NOT change that default; just report whether npm's restricted default is what callisto passes today.

TESTS: override + publishConfig.access=public → publish argv carries `--access public`; override with no publishConfig → unchanged; platform ops under that owner inherit it. Prove the key test fails without the fix.

RULES: `cargo test -p callisto-graph` (+ callisto-manifests if touched), then `cargo test -p callisto-cli` once. clippy -D warnings, fmt. Never `moon run`, never parallel cargo. One-line comments. Add `.changeset/publish-to-keeps-npm-access.md` (`callisto-cli: patch`), terse.

input.prompt:

Read .claude/plans/ROAD-TO-V1.md ("Agreed cuts", section 1 "GitHub App tag-push guard") first.

Three changes the owner approved. Commit each separately, each green.

1. REMOVE THE POST-PUBLISH RECEIPT PASS. crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs (~385-395): after `execute_release` returns with every op terminal, `observe_release_operations` (crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/capability.rs ~180-206) runs a fresh observation + recheck_trust per op, and `ReleaseReceiptV1::from_evidence` (callisto-model release.rs ~2410-2440) rejects on the first non-Exact. So one transient flake after everything is irreversibly published turns a successful release red with no receipt. Execution state already records per-op ExactEvidence at confirmation time (Confirmed / ObservedExactBeforeEffect / AdoptedExact transitions carry evidence). Build the receipt from the persisted state's evidence instead of re-observing. Keep every receipt invariant that still makes sense (complete roster, every op terminal-success, no duplicates); drop only the re-observation. If the state does NOT hold evidence for some role, STOP and report that rather than weakening the receipt. Decide receipt SCHEMA_VERSION per schema_guard_test and state it. Update tests that assumed re-observation.

2. TYPED DIAGNOSTIC FOR THE TAG-PUSH GUARD. GitHub refuses GITHUB_TOKEN (a GitHub App) pushing a tag whose commit's .github/workflows/ differs from every branch tip: remote message `refusing to allow a GitHub App to create or update workflow ... without \`workflows\` permission`. Today that surfaces as generic E164 + raw git stderr (provider/tag.rs push path ~87-100). Detect that message in the push failure and return a new GraphError with its own unused E-code (grep crates/ and docs/ to confirm unused; E179 is taken). Help text: this happens when releasing a commit that is not a branch tip (e.g. recovery of an older release) with GITHUB_TOKEN; push these tags with a non-App credential (list the exact tag names from the operation), then re-run recovery; GITHUB_TOKEN cannot be granted the workflows scope. Unit test via the fake runner with the exact stderr. Record the code in .claude/semantic-model/release-lifecycle.md E-codes.

3. RECOVERY RUNBOOK (docs only). docs/07-self-release-lifecycle.md: add a short "Recovering an older release" section: when tags can't be pushed by the workflow (the new diagnostic), push them manually as annotated tags at the release-source commit, then dispatch recovery; and when a recovery run reports ArtifactAssetDiffers after assets were already uploaded, delete the mismatched assets from the release and dispatch again (artifact observation treats a missing asset as absent; rebuilt tarballs are not byte-reproducible). Terse, exact commands.

RULES: `cargo test -p callisto-model -p callisto-graph` and `cargo test -p callisto-cli` once at the end. clippy -D warnings on touched crates, fmt. Never `moon run`, never parallel cargo. One-line comments, only non-obvious why. Changeset `.changeset/release-receipt-from-state.md` (`callisto-cli: minor` if receipt schema changes else patch) covering 1 and 2, terse. cargo fmt --all && mkdir -p .changeset && cat > .changeset/registry-observation-no-tool-retry.md <<'EOF'
---
callisto-cli: patch
---

**Unreachable registries are reported in seconds, not minutes**

Registry observation now turns off the package manager's own retries (`cargo --config net.retry=0 info`, `npm view --fetch-retries=0`) and relies on Callisto's bounded retry alone. Previously each of Callisto's attempts also retried inside cargo or npm, so an unreachable registry took about a minute (cargo) or six minutes (npm) before reporting indeterminate.
EOF
git status --short | grep '^??'; git add -A crates .changeset && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
fix(release): let callisto alone own registry observation retries

Registry observation ran cargo info and npm view with their default retries
inside each of callisto's bounded retry attempts. Measured against an
unreachable registry: cargo took ~11s per call (net.retry backoff) and npm ~70s
(fetch-retries), so five callisto attempts took about a minute and six minutes
respectively before reporting indeterminate. With the tool retries off: 0.1s
and 1s.

cargo only honours --config net.retry=0 as a global flag before the
subcommand; after `info` it is silently ignored (measured), so the argv puts it
first. The strict fake cargo, the argv allow-list check and the real-tool flag
contract now model that global flag, and red_d01 asserts every observation
disables cargo's retry. Also takes the unreachable-registry unit test from 58s
to 0.4s.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_019kLBz6zm7s9SLodEUj5oU9
EOF

=== main:.changeset/npm-platform-packages.md
---
callisto-cli: minor
---

**npm platform packages version with their owner**

An npm package with `os`/`cpu` that another npm package lists in `optionalDependencies` is now a platform manifest of that package, not a package of its own: it gets no tag, takes its owner's version, and the owner's `optionalDependencies` pins follow. This covers napi addons and native CLIs shipped esbuild-style, including `npm/<platform>` directories outside the workspace globs, which were previously ignored. Platform packages no longer need listing in a `[[fixed-group]]`. A workspace platform package with no single owner is reported as `platform-package-without-owner`.

A directory with both `Cargo.toml` and `package.json` now releases its npm side under the `package.json` name instead of the crate name.

`callisto release` publishes each attached platform package as a `platformPublish` operation of its owner, by directory (`npm publish <dir>` from the workspace root, whatever the package manager, since `--filter`/`workspace` only reach workspace members), with the owner's registry and access. Every platform publish must succeed before the owner's own npm publish runs; platform packages get no tag or GitHub Release. Release intents move to schema version 4: an intent planned by an earlier Callisto must be re-planned.

`plan-publish` lists attached platform packages by directory, and no longer reports a package that depends on a platform owner as missing a platform dependency.

Breaking (pre-1.0):
- A `Cargo.toml` + `package.json` directory whose names differ changes npm release identity, for example `npm/michi-node` becomes `npm/@orin-axi/michi`. Update `--package` selections, and re-run `callisto version --emit-decision` for any release-decision file committed before upgrading.
- A changeset naming an attached platform package (for example `"@s/cli-linux-x64-gnu": patch`) now reports an unknown package. Name the owner instead.
=== main:.changeset/pypi-observation.md
---
callisto-cli: minor
---

**PyPI publish targets work in durable releases**

`callisto release plan` no longer refuses PyPI. Versions are observed through the PEP 691 JSON simple index (`https://pypi.org/simple/<project>/`, or the configured private index) instead of `pip`, which cannot tell a missing project from an unreachable index. A yanked file reads as absent, so publishing over a yanked version fails closed. A private index that serves only PEP 503 HTML is reported as indeterminate; it must support the JSON simple index. Requires `curl` on the release runner.
=== main:.changeset/release-artifact-ownership.md
---
callisto-cli: minor
---

**Release artifacts are declared, not compiled in**

`[release] artifact-targets` is replaced by `[[release.artifact]]` entries, each naming the `package` that builds it, an opaque `target`, and its `asset-name`. Previously the four supported targets and their `callisto-*` asset names were compiled into Callisto and the configured list was validated then ignored, so no other workspace could use `[release]`. Any targets and names are now accepted; an asset-name must be unique and a single safe path component.

An artifact built by a package other than the product (for example a plugin shipped on the product's GitHub Release) is now recorded under that package in the release intent. Selecting one member of a `[[fixed-group]]` with `--package` now keeps its lockstep siblings in the release, so a sibling's artifact no longer fails with an unexplained "not authorized" error and no bumped sibling is left unpublished. That error now names the asset, its package and the fix.

Migrate each target to a block:

```toml
[[release.artifact]]
package = "cargo/my-cli"
target = "aarch64-apple-darwin"
asset-name = "my-cli-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz"
```
=== fix/registry-observation-no-tool-retry:.changeset/registry-observation-no-tool-retry.md
---
callisto-cli: patch
---

**Unreachable registries are reported in seconds, not minutes**

Registry observation now turns off the package manager's own retries (`cargo --config net.retry=0 info`, `npm view --fetch-retries=0`) and relies on Callisto's bounded retry alone. Previously each of Callisto's attempts also retried inside cargo or npm, so an unreachable registry took about a minute (cargo) or six minutes (npm) before reporting indeterminate.
=== fix/publish-to-keeps-npm-access:.changeset/publish-to-keeps-npm-access.md
---
callisto-cli: patch
---

**`publish-to = ["npm"]` no longer drops `publishConfig.access`/`registry`**

A `[[package]]`/`[[package-set]]` `publish-to = ["npm"]` override replaced the whole manifest-derived npm target, silently dropping `publishConfig.access` and `publishConfig.registry` read from `package.json`. A scoped package with no override-level access then published with npm's `restricted` default instead of the intended `public`, and the same dropped access was reused for any attached platform packages. The override now fills only the fields it doesn't itself set from the manifest; explicit config still wins.
=== refactor/release-cuts:.changeset/tag-push-workflow-guard.md
---
callisto-cli: patch
---

**Typed diagnostic for GitHub's workflow guard on tag push**

When GitHub refuses a release tag push because a GitHub App token (`GITHUB_TOKEN`) cannot push a commit whose `.github/workflows/` differs from every branch tip, `callisto release` now reports `E180` naming the tag and its target commit, with the remedy: push that tag with a non-App credential, then re-run recovery. It previously surfaced as a generic `E164` with raw git stderr. Other push failures are unchanged.

## Recovering an older release

Recovery of a release-source commit that is no longer a branch tip is an assisted procedure, not automation. Two platform facts block the unattended path.

**Tags the workflow cannot push (`E180`).** GitHub refuses a `GITHUB_TOKEN` push of any ref whose `.github/workflows/` differs from every branch tip, and no job permission grants the `workflows` scope. `E180` names the first refused tag and its commit; the run stops there, and every other tag of the release is refused the same way. ```sh

```sh
git tag -a "<tag>" -m "Release <tag>" "$SHA"   # once per tag of the release
git push origin "<tag>"
gh workflow run callisto-release.yml --ref main -f release_source_sha="$SHA"
```

**Assets that differ (`ArtifactAssetDiffers`).** Rebuilt tarballs are not byte-reproducible, so a recovery run that rebuilds artifacts reads assets uploaded by an earlier attempt as conflicting. Artifact observation treats a missing asset as absent, so delete the mismatched assets and dispatch again:

```sh
gh release delete-asset "<release tag>" "<asset name>" --yes   # once per mismatched asset
gh workflow run callisto-release.yml --ref main -f release_source_sha="$SHA"
```

content.text:
This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent

The goals, in order:
- **Initial:** fix Callisto's self-release after another agent "made a mess". The user chose "Audit #104 + release path", then asked to publish 0.8.0.
- **Architecture:** design for DX/UX, prefer zero-config with sane defaults, avoid overengineering, learn from prior art (changesets, knope, release-please, nx, cargo-dist, goreleaser), and support Rust, napi-rs and Python comprehensively.
- **Pre-1.0 work:** get to v1 soon, landing breaking changes now. Fix wiring gaps using agent teams with appropriate model and effort, parallelizing only where there is no conflict.
- **oxc:** support publishing oxc-react-docgen (napi) from `~/Projects/oxc-react-codegen`.
- **Builds:** speed up builds and tests. Ensure prod builds carry no debug symbols.
- **Cleanup:** remove stale worktrees. Run `cargo info` with zero retries.
- **Communication (latest):**
  - Be extremely succinct in all communication with the user and with agents.
  - Never hard-wrap PR descriptions or Markdown files.
  - Keep changesets, PR descriptions and docs succinct and free of AI slop and wordy prose.
- **Versioning:** pin versions (e.g. michi's `callisto-action@main`) only once safe versions exist.

2. Key Technical Concepts

**Release pipeline**
- Rust workspace driven by just/moon/proto. The self-release workflow `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml` runs: plan → build-artifact matrix → build → execute.
- GitHub Actions semantics:
  - A skipped ancestor skips any job without a status function.
  - `always()` runs a job even when the run is cancelled; `!cancelled()` does not.

# Release Lifecycle — Envelope, Evidence, Transitions

The three structural authorities of a durable release run. All three live in `callisto-model` (MIT, no Callisto dependencies); `callisto-graph` supplies provider adapters, `callisto-cli` supplies the run entry point.

## Run envelope (`release.rs`)

`ReleaseRunEnvelopeV1` is the immutable identity of one run: kind (`Initial`/`Recovery`), orchestration revision, release-source revision, profile, intent digest, artifact-manifest digest.

- One constructor, `ReleaseRunEnvelopeV1::new(kind, orchestration_revision, intent, manifest_digest)`. Profile, source revision, and intent digest are read out of the intent, so they have no second authority and cannot be asserted by a caller.
- Cross-field rules, enforced before the first effect: source revision equals the intent's Git source; manifest digest is `Some` exactly when the intent declares artifact slots; the orchestration revision equals every slot's attestation `workflow_commit`.
- It is persisted **inside** `ReleaseExecutionStateV1`, whose only constructor is `new(intent, envelope)`. The receipt is built from the state's envelope plus fresh observations — nothing is assembled after the effects.
- `validate_for_run` rejects state left by a different run (`ReleaseStateError::MismatchedEnvelope`, message names `--state`).

## Observation and evidence (`release_observation.rs`)

`ProviderObservationV1` is `Absent | Exact { evidence } | Conflict { reason } | Indeterminate { cause }`. `ProviderEvidenceV1` is closed and per-role: `RegistryVersion { version, checksum?, yanked? }`, `GitTag { peeled_commit }`, `ForgeRelease { tag_name, draft }`, `ArtifactUpload { byte_length, sha256 }`. `Option` fields are `None` where the adapter cannot yet prove the value. The `ForgeRelease` evidence serves both forge roles; for `ForgePublish` it is only accepted with `draft: false`.

`ReleaseOperationObservationV1::new` is the single constructor, used by deserialization too, and rejects evidence whose shape does not match the operation's role. Conflict reasons and indeterminate causes are closed enums; an authentication, rate-limit, or transport failure is always indeterminate, never a conflict.

Two tokens are mintable only from an observation: `AbsentProof` (from `Absent`) and `ExactEvidence` (from `Exact`).

## Registry observation through the package manager (`provider/registry.rs`)

Observation runs the ecosystem's own package manager -- the same tool and the same configuration the publish effect uses -- through the bounded `CommandRunner`, so registry resolution and authentication (private registries included) belong to the tool rather than to a credential-free reimplementation.

- cargo: `cargo info NAME@VERSION --registry REGISTRY`, run from the source workspace root so that workspace's `.cargo/config.toml` registry definitions and credentials apply. `--registry` is never omitted: without it `cargo info` resolves the local workspace and reports an unpublished member's on-disk version as published, which is the D01 defect. The logical `cratesIo` key maps to cargo's built-in `crates-io` (`cargo_registry_name`).
- npm: `npm view NAME@VERSION version --json`, reporting `checksum: None` rather than inventing one.
- npm platform packages (`os`/`cpu` set, listed in an owner's `optionalDependencies`) get a `PlatformPublish { registry, platform }` operation, published by directory before their owner.
- PyPI: `curl -sS -i` against the PEP 691 JSON simple index (not pip, which cannot tell a missing project from an unreachable index). 200 + matching file is `Exact`; a yanked file, no match, or 404 is `Absent` (fail closed, like cargo); transport failure or a non-JSON (PEP 503 HTML) body is `Indeterminate`. Parsed with the same `http::parse_http_response` as `gh api --include`.

Cargo classification (`classify_cargo_info`): exit 0 with a `version: VERSION` line for the requested version is `Exact` with `checksum: None, yanked: None` (`cargo info` reports neither, and the evidence does not invent them); exit 101 whose stderr carries ``could not find `NAME@VERSION` `` is `Absent`; anything else -- another exit code, another message, or a zero exit with no matching version line -- is a transient `Indeterminate` under the retry policy, so an unreachable registry can never read as an absence.

A **yanked** version reads as `Absent`, because `cargo info` answers "could not find" for one. This fails closed: the publish that follows is refused by the registry, and since only an `Exact` observation may satisfy an operation, the run ends in `RegistryPublishUnconfirmed`, never in a receipt. `ProviderConflictReason::RegistryVersionYanked` remains in the wire enum but no adapter currently produces it.

Registry endpoints must be `https` (`registry_endpoint::canonical_registry_url`), with no loopback exception, enforced identically by config load (E197 family) and release binding (E126).

## Forge roles and DAG order (`provider/forge.rs`, `provider/artifact.rs`)

Publication is the last forge step, because GitHub releases can be immutable: once published, assets can no longer be added, so a release must be complete before it is published.

`Tag` -> `ForgeRelease` (create as draft) -> every `ArtifactUpload` -> `ForgePublish`. `ForgePublish` depends on the draft and on *every* upload of that release, including when there are none.

- `ForgeRelease` effect: `gh release create TAG --repo R --verify-tag --draft --generate-notes`, plus `--prerelease` when the released version has a semver pre-release part (`Version::is_prerelease()`, the same source as the npm `next` dist-tag).
- `ForgePublish` effect: `gh release edit TAG --repo R --draft=false`.
- Lookup: `GET /releases/tags/{tag}` omits drafts, so a 404 there is followed by a bounded scan of `GET /releases?per_page=100&page=N` (at most 10 pages). Both roles and the upload role share this one lookup.
- `ForgeRelease` is `Exact` for a draft or a published release; `ForgePublish` is `Exact` only when `draft: false` and `Absent` while still a draft. A release whose tag matches but whose `prerelease` flag disagrees with the version is `Conflict { ForgeReleasePrereleaseDiffers }`.
- Uploads target the draft, compare by size and `sha256` digest, and never pass `--clobber`. An asset missing from a published release is `Absent`, so it is uploaded; an immutable release refuses that upload as a typed command failure rather than letting the release be reported complete.

## Artifact ownership (`config/resolve.rs`, `commands/release/derive.rs`)

A package is a dependency-graph node: versioned, cascaded, tagged, published. An artifact is a rendering of *(package, version, target)* into bytes. It has no tag, changelog or version of its own; it inherits them from its package.

- `[[release.artifact]]` declares `package`, an opaque `target` Callisto never parses, and a stable `asset-name`. Nothing about a product is compiled in.
- `ArtifactSlotId.package` is the package whose build produced the bytes, which need not be the product. Every slot still attaches to the product's one GitHub Release (the product's `ForgeRelease`/`ForgePublish`).
- `ArtifactSlotOutsideDecision` requires the owning package in the decision at the slot's version. `--package` narrowing therefore keeps every member of a selected package's `[[fixed-group]]` (membership from config, since the selected member's own reason is usually `Changeset`).
- Building is delegated. Callisto models the outputs and where they go, not how each ecosystem cross-compiles. napi platform packages and Python wheels go to their registries (publish path), not to `[release]`.

## Bounded retry (`provider/policy.rs`)

`retry_observation` wraps read-only observations only -- registry HTTP, the GitHub release GET, `git ls-remote`. An effect is never re-issued. Retryable: HTTP 429, any 5xx, a 403 carrying rate-limit headers, and a curl timeout or connection failure. Five attempts, 2s doubling to 16s, each wait capped at 300s, honouring `Retry-After` (delta-seconds or HTTP-date). Post-publish confirmation uses the same policy with `Absent` treated as index-propagation lag. `Sleeper` is the injected wall clock.

## Transition table (`release_transition.rs`)

`transition(current, event, run_kind)` is the only place an `OperationState` is computed; `ReleaseExecutionStateV1::apply` is the only mutator and takes the run kind from its own envelope. The whole legal edge set:

| From | Event | Kind | To |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pending | `Attempt { AbsentProof }` | any | Attempting |
| Pending | `ObservedExactBeforeEffect { ExactEvidence }` | any | AlreadySatisfied |
| Pending | `AdoptedExact { ExactEvidence }` | Recovery | AlreadySatisfied |
| Attempting | `Confirmed { ExactEvidence }` | any | Published |
| Attempting | `RecoveredExact { ExactEvidence }` | any | Published |
| Attempting | `EffectFailedAndAbsent { AbsentProof }` | any | Failed |
| Pending/Attempting | `Blocked { reason }` | any | Blocked |

Consequences: `Attempting` is unreachable without a proven-absent provider;
adopting a pre-existing effect into a missing journal is a recovery-only privilege; "our attempt landed" (`Published`) is distinct from "it already existed" (`AlreadySatisfied`); terminal states absorb every event.

## Fault-injection simulator (`commands/release_simulator.rs`)

A deterministic in-crate simulator drives the real `execute_release` plus the receipt path against an in-memory provider set and state writer, enumerating every crash point (each provider call, each save before and after) and every provider fault (indeterminate, conflict, effect-fails-before-landing, effect-lands-then-error, registry lag), then reruns as both the same runner and a fresh-journal recovery runner.

Asserted after every scenario: a receipt only over landed effects and a durable all-success journal; no effect re-issued for an operation already landed; no effect landing before every prerequisite; `Attempting` persisted only after an `Absent` observation in the same run; nothing downstream of an observed conflict landing; and convergence within three clean reruns -- except a same-runner rerun facing a persisted `Attempting` the provider does not hold, which is E173's deliberate refusal to re-dispatch, and a lost-journal recovery run re-issuing an effect a lagging index still reports absent, which only the provider can refuse.

## E-codes

- `E172` release execution incomplete (non-terminal operations remain).
- `E173` recovery unresolved: an `Attempting` or adopted operation is absent, conflicting, or indeterminate. Do not retry the effect.
- `E174` registry version already exists at preflight.
- `E176` provider indeterminate before dispatch.
- `E177` provider observation unusable as evidence (role mismatch; internal defect).
- `E178` run envelope invalid for this intent.
- `E179` an artifact's `package` is not part of this release (user config, not a defect).

`ReleaseExecutionStateV1::SCHEMA_VERSION` and `ReleaseReceiptV1::SCHEMA_VERSION` are both `2`; `ReleaseIntentV1::SCHEMA_VERSION` is `4` (the `platformPublish` role). I opened #119 for the test-suite speedup. Here's what it cuts:

| Change | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Release e2e tests no longer wait out real retry backoff | 35s per affected test | 5s |
| The moon wasm module is built once before tests, instead of test processes racing to build it | 127s for `moon_wasm_sandbox` | 83s |
| The wasm compiler (cranelift) is optimized even in dev builds | 17s for the first moon test | 9s |

These are the agent's local timings on this Mac, not CI. The rest of the moon tests still take about 6.5s each, which is mostly process startup, so this PR doesn't reduce them further.

To skip the backoff, the release binary now reads a test-only `__CALLISTO_TEST_SLEEP_SCALE` variable. It follows the same convention as cargo's `__CARGO_TEST_*` variables, and only the test harness sets it.

I cut the agent's long comments down to one line each and removed a redundant `rustup target add`. `rust-toolchain.toml` already declares the wasm target. After my edits, fmt, clippy and the 5s e2e test pass. The agent reported the graph, cli and moon test suites passing (1,000 tests together); I haven't rerun those since trimming the comments. CI will run them on the PR.

content.text:
It doesn't run on PRs. The workflow's only triggers are a push to `main` and a manual dispatch. Run 35779076723 was the push to `main` from merging #117 (event `push`, branch `main`).

On every push to `main` it does one of two things:
- **An ordinary PR was merged** (like #117): it creates or updates the release PR. That's the "Create or update the Callisto release PR" job, still in progress. The release jobs are skipped.
- **The release PR was merged**: it derives the release, builds the artifacts and publishes.

So it already behaves the way you describe. There's no separate trigger on the `callisto/version-packages` branch because the release PR is recomputed from `main` on every push.

One job may be wasted work: "Verify release candidate" reruns the full verification suite on every push to `main`, even though CI already ran on the PR. Two ways to cut it:
- Run it only when the release PR is merged, so publishing still gates on it.
- Drop it, since `main` already requires CI to pass before merging.
